claim: Kentucky recorded zero instances of corporal punishment in the 2023-24 school year after all 171 school districts adopted prohibiting policies by November 2, 2023, driven by a state board regulation rather than a statute.

sources.title: 704 KAR 7:170 Use of physical restraint and seclusion; corporal punishment
Kentucky records zero instances of corporal punishment during 2023-2024 school year
Kentucky Board of Education limits corporal punishment in schools
HB 22 (2020 Regular Session)

body:
Kentucky Board of Education regulation 704 KAR 7:170 (effective August 30, 2022) required every district to either prohibit corporal punishment or permit it only with annual written consent, per-instance verbal consent, a same-gender certified witness, no instruments, counseling within a day, and exclusions for students with IEPs or 504 plans, homeless and foster youth. Every district chose prohibition. Statewide incidents fell from about 1,100 in 2011-12 to 142 in 2019-20 to 5 in 2022-23. Ban bills (2020 HB 22 passed the House 65-17 and died in the Senate; 2022 HB 119 died in committee) never became law; the statute still permits the practice, so the map shows Kentucky as 'partial'.

claim: No study has found that ending corporal punishment increases misbehavior, and no study has found that using it improves behavior; as of September 2026 there is no US natural-experiment study of suspensions or achievement before and after a state or district ban.

sources.title: School corporal punishment in global perspective: Prevalence, outcomes, and efforts at intervention
Corporal punishment in schools (AAP policy statement)

body:
Both halves are accurate and the stronger causal claim is not supported. The 2023 AAP statement and Gershoff 2017 argue from the absence of any evidence of benefit plus the harm evidence. The training says exactly this and pairs abolition with PBIS and the Good Behavior Game so that paddling is not simply swapped for suspension. A district that publishes referral counts before and after its switch (training module 8) would produce the first such evidence.

claim: Seven federal circuits allow a student to sue over excessive corporal punishment under substantive due process ('shocks the conscience'), two under the Fourth Amendment, and the Fifth Circuit alone, covering Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, denies any federal claim where state remedies exist; the Supreme Court has declined to review that rule five times, most recently in January 2024.

sources.publisher: Institute for Justice / Supreme Court docket

body:
Substantive due process: Hall v. Tawney (4th Cir. 1980), Garcia v. Miera (10th Cir. 1987), Webb v. McCullough (6th Cir. 1987), Metzger v. Osbeck (3d Cir. 1988), Wise v. Pea Ridge (8th Cir. 1988, 855 F.2d 560), Neal v. Fulton County (11th Cir. 2000), Johnson v. Newburgh (2d Cir. 2001). Fourth Amendment: Wallace v. Batavia (7th Cir. 1995), Doe v. Hawaii DOE (9th Cir. 2003). Fifth Circuit: Fee v. Herndon (1990), T.O. v. Fort Bend ISD (2021, cert denied June 13, 2022), S.B. v. Jefferson Parish (2023, cert denied January 8, 2024 on an Institute for Justice petition). Strategy consequence: in the three states with the most paddling, the federal liability threat is the weakest in the country; liability arguments there must rest on state tort law, criminal law, and insurance, not on section 1983.

Texas, North Carolina and Georgia (physician letter only) remain opt-out states, where the burden is on the parent to object. Missouri: RSMo 160.261, SBs 681 and 662, effective August 28, 2022. Louisiana: R.S. 17:416.1(B), Act 268 of 2023 (HB 242), effective August 1, 2023, House 74-21, Senate 37-1. Florida: § 1002.20(4)(c), ch. 2025-110, effective July 1, 2025, final votes unanimous. Opt-in is the parental-rights bill and passes where bans fail; it also produces a signed form that can be counted.

claim: South Carolina's only statute on the subject, § 59-63-260, unchanged since 1973, says the governing body of each school district 'may provide corporal punishment for any pupil that it deems just and proper,' with no limits, and no bill to change it was filed in the 2023-24 or 2025-26 sessions.

What is the Department of Education's policy regarding corporal punishment?

body:
Federal data show 85 students struck in 2021-22 and 23 in 2017-18, so use is small but not zero. Whether every district has prohibited it by policy is unverified; a September 2025 Island Packet explainer likely has a current tally and should be read by a person (the site blocks agents).

claim: As of September 2026, corporal punishment in public schools is legal by statute in 17 states; in two of them, Kentucky and North Carolina, every district has prohibited it by policy, leaving 15 where it is both legal and in use.

sources.title: 15 states have laws that allow corporal punishment in schools
Letter from Secretary Cardona calling for an end to corporal punishment in schools
Country report: USA
sources.publisher: Global Initiative to End All Corporal Punishment of Children

body:
Counts differ by source because states with no statute either way (Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Maine) are classified differently: Cardona 2023 counted 23 (16 expressly allow, 7 do not prohibit); Bellwether 2024 said 17; APSAC 2025 said 18; NPR's August 2026 tracker said 15 allow and 30 plus DC ban. This project's list (data/states/) is: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Wyoming. No state enacted a full public-school ban in 2024, 2025, or 2026 (searched 2026-09-09); the most recent are Colorado and Idaho (2023).

claim: Wyoming's statute does not authorize corporal punishment outright; it grants school staff civil and criminal immunity for 'reasonable corporal discipline' authorized by board policy, and bills to repeal that immunity failed in the House in 2023 (12-47) and failed introduction in 2026 (38-24, short of two-thirds).

sources.title: Wyoming Statutes Title 21 (§ 21-4-308)
SF0047 (2023) Education, repeal of immunity for corporal discipline
HB0065 (2026) K-12 public school discipline
A Sheridan County school principal is seeking to end corporal punishment in Wyoming's public schools

body:
W.S. § 21-4-308(b). By 2022-23, press reported only one to three of Wyoming's 48 districts still had corporal punishment in policy (Niobrara County School District #1 named), and the state had reported no incidents to the federal government since 2012; the 2022 and 2023 district counts conflict. Laramie County SD 1 reaffirmed its prohibition in October 2025. The advocate was a middle-school principal, Jeff Jones, whose dissertation reviewed all 48 policies.

claim: In October 2023 a Texas judge dismissed the assault charge against an Overton ISD principal who had paddled a student hard enough to leave bruising a child-abuse physician called consistent with abuse, because district policy was followed and the mother was present and consenting.

sources.title: Rusk County judge dismisses assault charge against Overton principal
Teacher, assistant principal charged following investigation into paddling incident

body:
The clearest recent illustration that in a paddling state the law protects the paddler, not the child, when policy is followed. Other 2022-26 matters: Jackson County, Tennessee, teacher and assistant principal indicted November 2023 after two paddlings injured a student (outcome not found); East Jasper, Mississippi, third-grader's arm fractured February 2025 (no action found); no published civil settlement for school paddling was found in the period.
